instruments_tools.desc: Measurement instruments, scales and coding protocols used to assess social competence: standardized questionnaires (e.g., Social Skills Rating System, Social Skills Inventory, Interpersonal Competence Questionnaire, Strengths and Difficulties Questionnaire subscales where applicable), observational coding schemes (e.g., peer interaction coding), structured interviews, vignettes and intervention manuals designed to measure or train social competence.
instruments_tools.narr: Relevant: validated psychometric instruments, observational coding schemes, structured interview guides, training/intervention manuals and questionnaires that are intended to assess or change social competence. Include instrument documentation, scoring keys and reliability/validity information. Not relevant: generic personality inventories without clear social-competence subscales, instruments that assess organizational competencies, or tools that only measure unrelated constructs (e.g., academic skills) unless they include explicit social competence modules.

publication.desc: Publications on social work (soziale Arbeit): theory, history, professional practice, methods, ethics, policy, education and training, empirical evaluations of social work interventions, case studies and program reports in community, clinical, school, child welfare, mental health, geriatric and other social service settings.
publication.narr: Relevant: books, journal articles, reports and theses whose primary focus is social work practice, education, policy or research (including program evaluations and professional guidelines). Include both German- and English-language works that address social work at micro, mezzo and macro levels. Not relevant: documents that use the phrase 'social work' incidentally (e.g., volunteer community activities) without professional/practice focus, or publications about adjacent disciplines (e.g., social policy, sociology) unless they centrally address social work roles, interventions or workforce issues.

research_data.desc: Datasets related to social work practice and services: case management records (anonymized), administrative records from child welfare, social service utilization data, evaluation datasets from social work interventions, needs assessments, surveys of social workers and clients, and longitudinal studies of client outcomes.
research_data.narr: Relevant: data collections used to study social work processes, client outcomes from social services, workforce surveys of social workers, evaluation trials of social work interventions and administrative datasets from social service agencies. Include documentation and metadata enabling reuse. Not relevant: general population surveys without identifiable social work variables, clinical trial data unrelated to social service contexts, or raw administrative data without documentation enabling identification of social work-related variables.

variables.desc: Variables commonly used in social work research and practice: client demographics, case type (e.g., child protection, homelessness), service utilization, referral source, intervention type, case outcomes (safety, well-being, housing stability), risk assessments, functional status, social worker caseload and qualifications, service duration and intensity.
variables.narr: Relevant: variables that document client needs, interventions, outcomes and social worker characteristics used in social work contexts (e.g., 'case_open_date', 'service_type', 'risk_score', 'housing_status_at_followup'). Include variables from administrative, survey and evaluation datasets. Not relevant: variables that do not pertain to social service delivery or client outcomes (e.g., purely economic indicators) unless explicitly linked to social work practice.

instruments_tools.desc: Assessment tools, screening instruments, practice manuals and software used in social work: risk assessment tools, needs assessment instruments, standardized outcome measures (e.g., Outcome Rating Scale, HoNOS where used in social care), case management systems, intervention manuals, supervision tools and professional competency frameworks for social workers.
instruments_tools.narr: Relevant: validated screening/assessment instruments, intervention manuals, measurement scales and software platforms used specifically in social work settings or evaluated for social work practice. Include documentation, scoring guides and implementation protocols. Not relevant: general healthcare instruments unrelated to social care, or managerial software unrelated to client-facing social work activities.

publication.desc: Publications addressing social media use (soziale Medien Nutzung): empirical and theoretical studies on patterns, motives, frequency, intensity, platform-specific behaviors, impacts on mental health, political communication, identity, privacy, digital literacy and media effects across populations.
publication.narr: Relevant: studies and reviews that explicitly investigate how people use social media (usage patterns, motives, time spent, active vs passive use, platform choice), including experimental, survey, qualitative and mixed-methods research. Include policy reports and media-usage trend analyses. Not relevant: publications about social media platforms' technical architecture without user-behavior focus, or broad 'social media' mentions that do not examine user use or user-related outcomes.

research_data.desc: Datasets capturing social media use: self-report survey data about use patterns and motives, longitudinal panels on digital media behavior, digital trace data (API extracts, logs, screen-time measures), time-use datasets with social media variables and multimodal datasets combining surveys with passive measurement.
research_data.narr: Relevant: datasets that quantify or qualify social media usage (frequency, duration, platform-specific metrics, engagement measures, content interactions), including both self-report and passive-tracking data, with documentation on collection methods and consent. Not relevant: data about social media companies' internal metrics without user-level behaviors, datasets only about general internet access without social media variables, or raw platform data lacking ethical/consent documentation.

variables.desc: Variables that operationalize social media use: frequency (daily/weekly), duration (minutes/hours), number of logins, platform-specific use (Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, Twitter/X), active vs passive use, posting frequency, types of content engaged with, motives for use, self-reported multitasking while using, and metrics of engagement (likes, comments, shares).
variables.narr: Relevant: variables explicitly measuring social media behaviors (e.g., 'instagram_minutes_per_day', 'posts_per_week', 'passive_use_index', 'motivation_social_connection'), including derived engagement metrics. Not relevant: variables that only indicate internet access or device ownership without measurable social media use, or platform-agnostic labels that cannot be mapped to usage behavior.

instruments_tools.desc: Measurement instruments and tools for assessing social media use: questionnaires and scales (e.g., Social Media Use Integration Scale, Bergen Social Media Addiction Scale variants, bespoke usage questionnaires), passive data collection tools (screen-time apps, browser/mobile logging scripts), API extraction tools, content-coding schemes and protocols for classifying user activities.
instruments_tools.narr: Relevant: validated scales, survey items and passive-tracking tools designed to measure social media usage and related behaviors, plus coding manuals for content and engagement classification and scripts for ethical API data collection. Not relevant: generic internet-use instruments without social media specificity, or developer-focused platform tools that do not collect user-behavior data.

publication.desc: Publications on social media (soziale Medien) broadly: studies of platforms, content, users, societal effects (misinformation, political mobilization, public health communication), business models, regulation, governance, platform design, digital culture and cross-cutting theoretical work on social media phenomena.
publication.narr: Relevant: empirical and theoretical works that focus on social media platforms, their societal roles, user practices, content dynamics, governance and policy implications, including interdisciplinary perspectives (communication, sociology, political science, media studies). Not relevant: papers that only mention social media in passing or focus solely on unrelated technologies without engagement with social media's societal/user aspects.

research_data.desc: Datasets related to social media content and dynamics: platform-derived datasets (posts, comments, network ties), content annotations (topic labels, misinformation flags), engagement metrics, comparative corpora across platforms, and combined datasets linking social media content to surveys or administrative data.
research_data.narr: Relevant: datasets containing social media content, metadata, interaction networks, annotated corpora and integrated datasets linking social media activity with external measures (e.g., election results, health indicators). Include documentation on collection methods and ethical considerations. Not relevant: datasets that only reference social media at a high level without content/interaction data, or proprietary/platform-internal datasets inaccessible for research.

variables.desc: Variables capturing social media phenomena: content attributes (text, hashtags, multimedia tags), engagement counts (likes, shares, comments), temporal metadata, user attributes (anonymized demographics, follower counts), network measures, sentiment/topic labels, misinformation indicators and platform-affordance variables (algorithmic recommendation exposure).
variables.narr: Relevant: variables that represent social media content, user interactions and network properties (e.g., 'tweet_timestamp', 'likes_count', 'retweet_network_degree', 'sentiment_label', 'misinformation_flag'). Not relevant: generic social variables not tied to social media content/interaction or variables lacking provenance/definition making them unusable for analysis.

instruments_tools.desc: Tools and instruments for social media research: data collection tools (APIs, scraping frameworks), annotation platforms, coding schemes for content analysis, sentiment and topic modeling pipelines, network analysis software and ethical/consent protocols and guidelines for social media research.
instruments_tools.narr: Relevant: documented software, scripts, methodological protocols and coding manuals used to collect, preprocess, annotate and analyze social media data, including ethical guidelines. Not relevant: undocumented scraping code without reproducible methods, corporate proprietary analytic tools not intended for academic research, or instruments unrelated to social media content/interaction analysis.

publication.desc: Publications on social networks (soziale Netzwerke): theoretical and empirical work on interpersonal and organizational networks, network structure and dynamics, social network analysis (SNA) methods, friendship/communication networks, diffusion processes, homophily, centrality and applications in sociology, epidemiology, organizational studies and online networks.
publication.narr: Relevant: works focusing on social network theory, methodology and empirical analyses of ties among actors (individuals, groups, organizations), including studies of network formation, diffusion, influence and structural properties. Include both offline and online network studies. Not relevant: papers that use the phrase 'network' metaphorically without analysis of relational ties or graph-structured data, or purely technical network-engineering topics unrelated to social relations.

research_data.desc: Network datasets: adjacency matrices, edge lists, ego-networks and whole-network data (offline and online), temporal/dynamic networks, multiplex networks, labeled ties, and linked actor attributes used for SNA and diffusion studies, with accompanying metadata and collection protocols.
research_data.narr: Relevant: datasets representing relational ties among actors suitable for SNA (e.g., friendship matrices, communication logs, collaboration networks), including longitudinal and multiplex network data and documentation on tie definition and sampling. Not relevant: datasets that only contain individual-level variables without relational ties, or network-like data from technical/IT networks (e.g., packet flows) not mapping to social relations.

variables.desc: Variables and measures used in social network research: tie existence and strength, tie directionality, frequency of interaction, role indicators, actor attributes, network-level measures (density, centralization), node-level centrality measures (degree, betweenness, eigenvector), homophily indices, and temporal tie attributes.
variables.narr: Relevant: variables that specify relationships between actors (e.g., 'edge_weight', 'contact_frequency', 'mentor_pairing'), and derived SNA measures at node and network levels. Include variable metadata defining tie construction and measurement. Not relevant: isolated individual variables not linked to relational data, or network-terminology used outside of relational analysis contexts.

instruments_tools.desc: SNA instruments and tools: survey name-generator and roster instruments for eliciting ties, observational protocols for recording interactions, software and libraries for network analysis and visualization (e.g., UCINET, Gephi, igraph, NetworkX), statistical packages for ERGM/SAOM/temporal models and guideline documents for network data collection and anonymization.
instruments_tools.narr: Relevant: validated network elicitation instruments (name-generator questionnaires), coding protocols for interaction observation, and documented software/tools/methods for network construction, analysis and visualization, including privacy/anonymization best practices. Not relevant: generic graph-theory tools intended for non-social networks (e.g., electrical or computer networks) without adaptation to social-science data collection or interpretation.

publication.desc: Publications (articles, books, reports) on social mobility and status change across generations or life-course, including educational, occupational and income mobility; comparative and national studies, mobility theory and measurement.
publication.narr: Include empirical and theoretical works that investigate change in social status between origin and destination (intergenerational mobility) or within individual life-courses (intra‑generational mobility). Relevant studies address determinants and consequences of upward/downward mobility, mobility tables and indices, cohort comparisons, and policy-related analyses. Exclude literature focusing on spatial/geographic mobility (migration, commuting) or unrelated uses of the term 'mobility' (e.g. physical mobility in health) unless social/occupational status change is central.

research_data.desc: Microdata collections and longitudinal datasets containing origin and destination socioeconomic indicators (parental education/occupation/income and respondent’s education/occupation/income) suitable for measuring mobility.
research_data.narr: Include panel and retrospective data that permit construction of mobility matrices or mobility indices (e.g. SOEP, longitudinal cohort studies, national microcensus modules, ESS with retrospective questions). Data must allow linking parental/background characteristics to adult outcomes by cohort or birth-year to analyse intergenerational mobility. Exclude datasets without origin or destination socioeconomic measures or those focused solely on geographic movement.

variables.desc: Socioeconomic origin and destination variables: parental education, parental occupation/class, household income in childhood, respondent education, respondent occupation/class, current income, social class codes and mobility indicators (transition matrices, mobility indices).
variables.narr: Include variables that operationalize social origin (father/mother education and occupation, childhood household resources) and social destination (respondent’s education, occupational status, income, class). Also include derived variables used to measure mobility such as intergenerational status tables, relative/absolute mobility rates, odds ratios, Shorrocks/Gini mobility measures, ISEI/ISEI changes. Exclude variables that only measure physical movement or unrelated demographic traits.

instruments_tools.desc: Coding schemes and tools used to measure and analyse social mobility: occupational classification systems (ISCO, ISCO-08, ISEI, EGP), mobility matrices, statistical scripts/packages for mobility analysis, survey modules on social origin.
instruments_tools.narr: Include instruments that support consistent measurement of origin and destination (standard occupational classifications, socio‑economic index conversions, questionnaires capturing parental background), as well as analysis tools (R/SPSS/Stata routines for constructing mobility tables and mobility indices). Exclude measurement instruments unrelated to social/occupational status (e.g. physical mobility trackers).

publication.desc: Publications addressing social origin, family background and their effects on educational attainment, labour market outcomes, cultural capital, health and inequality.
publication.narr: Include empirical studies and theoretical treatments on how parental socioeconomic status, education, occupation, and family resources shape life chances (education, employment, health). Works on intergenerational transmission, social reproduction, childhood context and policy interventions are relevant. Exclude publications that use 'origin' only in a geographic or non‑socioeconomic sense without considering family background or childhood socioeconomic indicators.

research_data.desc: Datasets containing measures of family background and childhood circumstances (parental education/occupation, household income, material resources, cultural capital indicators, migration background).
research_data.narr: Include surveys and cohorts that collect parental and childhood information (e.g. SOEP, NEPS, PISA, microcensus modules, cohort studies) enabling analysis of effects of social origin on later outcomes. Prefer data with retrospective childhood modules or linked parent–child information. Exclude data lacking any parental/background indicators or only capturing place of birth without family socioeconomic measures.

variables.desc: Variables capturing parental and childhood socioeconomic characteristics: parental education, parental occupation/class, parental income, household conditions in childhood, number of books in the home, parental employment, migration background, family structure.
variables.narr: Include direct measures of parents' socioeconomic status and proxy indicators of cultural and material resources in childhood used to operationalize social origin. Also include derived SES indices and categorical class measures. Exclude variables unrelated to family background such as contemporary individual attitudes unless used as mediators or outcomes of social origin.

instruments_tools.desc: Survey modules, question items and coding schemes for measuring social origin (retrospective childhood modules, parental occupation/education items, SES composite indices) and conversion tools for standard class/SES measures.
instruments_tools.narr: Include validated questionnaire items and modules used to elicit parental education/occupation, household conditions in childhood, and cultural capital (e.g. number of books), as well as tools to map occupations to standard classifications (ISCO, ISEI, EGP) to derive SES measures. Exclude instruments that measure only adult SES without retrospective or parental information.

publication.desc: Publications on socio‑political attitudes and values, including political ideology, policy preferences, political trust, party identification, civic attitudes and public opinion research.
publication.narr: Include research examining the nature, distribution, determinants and consequences of socio‑political attitudes (e.g. left–right orientation, policy issue positions, authoritarian attitudes, trust in institutions). Comparative and national public opinion studies, longitudinal attitude change, and work linking social characteristics to political attitudes are relevant. Exclude studies that address social behaviours without linking to political attitudes or those focused solely on non‑political social attitudes.

research_data.desc: Survey data sources that measure political and social attitudes at individual level (e.g. ALLBUS, ESS, Eurobarometer, CSES, national election studies, Politbarometer, panel surveys with political modules).
research_data.narr: Include cross‑sectional and panel datasets containing standard items on ideology, party choice, political trust, policy preferences, civic engagement and related socio‑demographic covariates. Data should allow analysis of attitude distributions, correlates, and change over time. Exclude datasets without political attitude measures or that only include aggregated electoral returns without individual-level responses.

variables.desc: Variables measuring political and social attitudes: left–right self-placement, party preference, political trust, policy issue positions (immigration, welfare, environment), social values, voting intention/behavior, civic engagement indicators.
variables.narr: Include standard attitude items and scales used to operationalize socio‑political views (e.g. Likert items on policy preferences, trust scales, ideological self-placement) and demographic covariates used to explain variation. Also include composite scales (authoritarianism, social conservatism). Exclude purely behavioral variables without attitudinal content unless used as outcomes of attitudes.

instruments_tools.desc: Standardized questionnaire modules, validated scales and coding schemes used to measure political attitudes and values (ESS political items, CSES modules, party identification questions, trust scales).
instruments_tools.narr: Include survey instruments and batteries commonly used in public opinion research (e.g. ESS questionnaire modules, CSES items, Likert scales for trust and policy positions), plus codebooks and harmonization tools for cross‑national comparison. Exclude instruments that do not capture political attitudes or that only measure unrelated social traits.

publication.desc: Publications on sport and physical activity, including sports sociology, sport participation, public health studies on physical activity, organized sport, youth sport and sports policy.
publication.narr: Include research that examines participation rates, determinants of sport involvement, effects of sport on health and social outcomes, sport club membership, elite sport and policy/intervention studies promoting physical activity. Both population‑level and specialized studies (e.g. youth sports, gender differences) are relevant. Exclude literature solely about sports history or biographical material unless it bears on social or health research questions.

research_data.desc: Datasets measuring sport participation and physical activity (surveys and health studies with sport modules, e.g. national health surveys, Eurobarometer sport/physical activity modules, sport-specific surveys and fitness studies).
research_data.narr: Include cross‑sectional and panel data that record frequency, type, duration and intensity of sport or physical activity, club membership and related socio‑demographic variables. Relevant sources include national health surveys (e.g. DEGS), sport participation surveys and international comparative datasets. Exclude datasets that do not contain sport/physical activity measures or only administrative records of elite sport without population participation data.

variables.desc: Variables on sport and physical activity: participation (yes/no), frequency, duration, intensity, type of sport, club membership, informal activity, barriers to participation, competitive level.
variables.narr: Include standard measures used to operationalize sport behaviour (weekly frequency, minutes of activity, METs, membership indicators), as well as contextual variables (facility access, socio‑demographics). Also include objective activity measures where available (accelerometer counts). Exclude unrelated fitness biomarkers unless explicitly linked to sport behaviour.

instruments_tools.desc: Measurement instruments and tools for sport and physical activity: standardized questionnaires (IPAQ, Global Physical Activity Questionnaire), sport participation modules, accelerometers and activity trackers, fitness tests and codebooks for sport survey modules.
instruments_tools.narr: Include validated self‑report instruments (IPAQ, GPAQ), device-based measurement protocols (accelerometer wear protocols), and survey modules used in major health and sport surveys. Also include coding manuals for classifying sport types and intensity. Exclude recreational activity measures that are not about sport or physical activity unless integrated into broader activity instruments.

publication.desc: Publications on teacher stress, burnout, workload, occupational health of teachers, classroom-related stressors and interventions to reduce stress in educational settings.
publication.narr: Include empirical studies, reviews and intervention evaluations that focus on stress, psychological strain, burnout and well‑being among teachers at all levels (primary, secondary, vocational). Relevant topics include causes (workload, class size, student behaviour), consequences (absenteeism, turnover), and prevention/therapy. Exclude studies on student stress or general occupational stress not specifically addressing teachers.

research_data.desc: Survey and administrative datasets that include measures of teacher stress, burnout, mental health, working conditions and organizational factors (e.g. TALIS, national teacher surveys, occupational health studies with teacher subsamples).
research_data.narr: Include datasets with occupation-specific modules for teachers measuring perceived stress, burnout scales, workload, support and classroom conditions (e.g. OECD TALIS, national education workforce surveys, teacher panels). Data should allow linking stress to organizational or student-related variables. Exclude datasets lacking teacher identifiers or any measures of stress/psychosocial working conditions.

variables.desc: Variables capturing teacher stress and related constructs: perceived stress, burnout dimensions (emotional exhaustion, depersonalization, reduced personal accomplishment), workload, time pressure, classroom management difficulties, support from colleagues/management, absenteeism, job satisfaction.
variables.narr: Include validated psychometric measures (subscales or items) and contextual variables that explain or result from stress (work hours, class size, student behaviour). Also include outcome variables such as sick leave, intention to leave and mental health indicators. Exclude generic stress proxies that are not tied to the teaching occupation unless occupation is specified.

instruments_tools.desc: Validated instruments and survey modules for assessing teacher stress and burnout: Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI), Perceived Stress Scale (PSS), Teacher Stress Inventory (TSI), COPSOQ, TALIS teacher questionnaire items and related occupational health tools.
instruments_tools.narr: Include standardized scales and questionnaire modules commonly used to measure teacher stress and psychosocial working conditions, as well as protocols for occupational health assessments in schools. Also include intervention tools and evaluation instruments designed for teacher well‑being. Exclude general stress instruments without occupational adaptation unless applied specifically to teacher samples.

publication.desc: Publications on psychological, physical and work-related stress among nursing staff in hospitals, long‑term care, and community nursing, including prevalence studies, risk factor analyses, and intervention evaluations.
publication.narr: Include: empirical articles, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, theses and practice guidelines that focus on stress experienced by nurses or nursing aides (acute care, long‑term care, home care), studies of work environment determinants (staffing, shift work, patient acuity), and evaluations of stress‑reduction interventions for nursing staff. Include mixed‑methods and qualitative studies describing lived experience of stress in nursing. Include German and English publications. Exclude: studies of general population stress without nursing focus, stress in non‑human subjects, publications that only mention nursing as a secondary, incidental subgroup without separate results for nurses.

research_data.desc: Datasets and study data related to stress among nursing personnel: survey data, longitudinal cohort data, observational studies, and intervention trial datasets that measure stress or related outcomes in nursing populations.
research_data.narr: Include: datasets from cross‑sectional and longitudinal occupational health surveys of nurses, workplace intervention trials (randomized or quasi‑experimental) targeting stress reduction in nursing, qualitative interview/transcript datasets from nurses on stress, administrative data linking staffing/shift patterns to stress outcomes, and physiological datasets collected in nursing samples (e.g., cortisol) if tied to psychological stress measures. Exclude: datasets that do not include nurses or that do not measure stress, and anonymized aggregated hospital statistics without individual stress measures.

variables.desc: Variables capturing perceived stress, job demands in nursing, working conditions, mental and physical health outcomes, and potential moderators/mediators specific to nursing.
variables.narr: Include: perceived stress scales (PSS), nursing‑specific stress measures (e.g., Nursing Stress Scale), workload measures (patient‑nurse ratio, acuity), shift characteristics (night work, rotation), staffing levels, exposure to traumatic events, burnout indicators, sleep quality, depression/anxiety screening scores, sick leave/absenteeism, turnover intention, social support at work, coping strategies, and intervention exposure. Exclude: generic physiological measures without linkage to psychological stress or variables unrelated to occupational stress (e.g., unrelated clinical biomarkers collected for other purposes).

instruments_tools.desc: Validated questionnaires and assessment tools commonly used to measure stress, burnout, workload and coping in nursing contexts, plus organizational assessment instruments and intervention materials targeting nurse stress.
instruments_tools.narr: Include: Perceived Stress Scale (PSS), Nursing Stress Scale (NSS), Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI), Copenhagen Psychosocial Questionnaire (COPSOQ), effort‑reward imbalance (ERI) measures, Job Content Questionnaire (JCQ), sleep and fatigue scales, Brief COPE and other coping inventories used in nursing samples, observational checklists for workload/acuity, stress‑reduction program manuals (mindfulness, resilience training) evaluated in nursing. Exclude: instruments that are not validated for occupational or nursing contexts or instruments solely for clinical diagnosis not used to assess occupational stress.

publication.desc: Publications addressing work‑related stress among employees across sectors, covering determinants, prevalence, health and productivity outcomes, and workplace interventions.
publication.narr: Include: empirical studies, reviews, policy papers and reports on occupational stress among employees (private and public sectors), studies using job stress models (demand‑control, ERI), research on consequences (mental/physical health, absenteeism, presenteeism, turnover), and evaluations of workplace interventions. Include German and English sources and sector‑specific studies if they report results for employees. Exclude: studies on students, retirees, or non‑working populations without employee data; animal or purely biological stress studies without an occupational context.

research_data.desc: Employee‑level datasets measuring occupational stress, working conditions, and related outcomes from company surveys, national labour studies, cohort studies and intervention evaluations.
research_data.narr: Include: company or sector surveys on psychosocial working conditions, national occupational health datasets, longitudinal cohort data linking job characteristics to health outcomes, administrative HR data linked to stress measures (sick leave, turnover), and datasets from trials of workplace stress interventions. Exclude: data that do not contain measures of work‑related stress or that only include non‑employee populations.

variables.desc: Workplace variables reflecting psychosocial stressors and employee outcomes: job demands, control, support, working hours, contract type, job insecurity, stress perception, health and productivity indicators.
variables.narr: Include: job demands, decision latitude/control, social support at work, effort‑reward imbalance, working hours/overtime, shift work, job insecurity, workplace harassment/bullying, perceived stress measures (PSS), burnout, depression/anxiety scales, absenteeism, presenteeism, performance, health service utilization, and demographic/workplace covariates (occupation, sector). Exclude: variables unrelated to employment (e.g., childhood stressors) unless explicitly modeled as mediators/moderators in employee stress research.

instruments_tools.desc: Standardized instruments for assessing job stressors and employee stress outcomes and organizational assessment tools used in occupational health and BGM contexts.
instruments_tools.narr: Include: Job Content Questionnaire (JCQ), Effort‑Reward Imbalance (ERI) questionnaire, Copenhagen Psychosocial Questionnaire (COPSOQ), Perceived Stress Scale (PSS), Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI), HSE Management Standards Indicator Tool, instruments measuring absenteeism/presenteeism (e.g., WHO‑HPQ), and workplace survey toolkits used in occupational health research. Exclude: clinical instruments unrelated to occupational functioning or tools lacking validation for work settings.

publication.desc: Publications on the relationship between stress and coping processes, including types of coping, efficacy, coping interventions, and how coping moderates or mediates stress–outcome relations.
publication.narr: Include: empirical studies, longitudinal research, experimental work, systematic reviews and meta‑analyses investigating coping strategies (problem‑focused, emotion‑focused, avoidance), coping effectiveness, coping as mediator/moderator between stress and health, and interventions to improve coping skills. Include studies across populations (workers, patients, students) if they report explicit stress–coping relationships. Exclude: papers that discuss coping only tangentially, or studies of physiological stress responses without psychological coping measures.

research_data.desc: Datasets capturing both stress exposures and coping responses: surveys, diary studies, experimental data, and intervention trial data that assess coping and stress outcomes.
research_data.narr: Include: cross‑sectional and longitudinal survey data with coping and stress measures, ecological momentary assessment (EMA)/diary datasets tracking stress and coping in real time, intervention datasets testing coping training, and clinical trial data where coping is an outcome or mediator. Exclude: datasets lacking coping measures or only measuring coping vaguely without validated scales.

variables.desc: Variables measuring perceived stress/appraisal, specific coping strategies, coping efficacy, and downstream outcomes (mental health, physiological responses), plus situational/contextual moderators.
variables.narr: Include: perceived stress and appraisal measures, coping style scores (problem‑focused, emotion‑focused, avoidance), coping subscales (e.g., active coping, seeking social support, denial), coping efficacy/self‑efficacy, measures of reappraisal, rumination, emotion regulation, outcomes such as depression, anxiety, burnout, physiological stress markers when linked to coping, and contextual variables (social support, resources). Exclude: non‑specific or single‑item measures of coping that do not distinguish strategy types.

instruments_tools.desc: Validated coping inventories and stress appraisal tools commonly used to assess coping processes, plus intervention manuals for coping skills training and diaries/EMA tools.
instruments_tools.narr: Include: COPE Inventory and Brief COPE, Ways of Coping Questionnaire, Coping Orientation to Problems Experienced, Response to Stress Questionnaire (RSQ), Perceived Stress Scale (PSS) for appraisal, measures of emotion regulation (e.g., ERQ), standardized diary/EMA protocols for momentary coping assessment, and manuals for cognitive‑behavioral or mindfulness‑based coping interventions. Exclude: ad‑hoc single‑item measures or instruments not validated for assessing coping strategies.

publication.desc: Research on the association between stress and burnout, including etiological studies, prevalence, longitudinal trajectories, risk and protective factors, and intervention effectiveness for preventing or reducing burnout.
publication.narr: Include: empirical studies and reviews that examine how workplace or life stressors contribute to burnout, longitudinal studies tracking stress and development of burnout, interventions aimed at reducing stress to prevent burnout, and studies identifying mediators/moderators (coping, resources). Include occupation‑specific research (healthcare, teaching, social work) where stress–burnout links are analyzed. Exclude: studies mentioning burnout without measuring stress, clinical case reports unrelated to occupational or chronic stress exposure, and research on transient fatigue not conceptualized as burnout.

research_data.desc: Datasets containing measures of stress and validated burnout scales, including longitudinal cohorts, occupational surveys, and intervention trial data assessing burnout outcomes.
research_data.narr: Include: workplace and cohort datasets with both stressor measures and burnout outcomes (MBI, CBI, OLBI), longitudinal data suitable for temporal analyses of stress predicting burnout, randomized and non‑randomized intervention datasets evaluating stress reduction and burnout change, and administrative HR data linked to burnout measures. Exclude: datasets without validated burnout measures or without measures of stressors/appraisals.

variables.desc: Variables assessing stress exposure/appraisal, burnout dimensions, job and personal risk/protective factors, health outcomes and occupational consequences.
variables.narr: Include: measures of perceived stress, objective stressors (workload, emotional demands), burnout subscales (emotional exhaustion, depersonalization/cynicism, reduced personal accomplishment), coping strategies, social support, job resources, sleep, depression/anxiety, absenteeism, turnover intention, and physiological stress markers when analyzed in relation to burnout. Exclude: general well‑being indices not linked to stress or burnout constructs.

instruments_tools.desc: Validated instruments to measure stress and burnout and intervention materials targeting stress reduction and burnout prevention/rehabilitation.
instruments_tools.narr: Include: Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI), Copenhagen Burnout Inventory (CBI), Oldenburg Burnout Inventory (OLBI), Perceived Stress Scale (PSS), COPSOQ, job stress instruments (JCQ, ERI), measures of sleep/fatigue, and manuals for workplace interventions (CBT, resilience training, organizational interventions) aimed at reducing stress and burnout. Exclude: burnout measures not validated or studies using informal/unstandardized burnout proxies without psychometric support.

publication.desc: Publications on workplace health management (BGM) interventions, programs and policies that address stress prevention, reduction and promotion of mental health in organizations.
publication.narr: Include: evaluations of BGM programs, implementation studies, guidelines and best‑practice reports focusing explicitly on stress reduction or mental health promotion in the workplace, cost‑effectiveness analyses, and studies of organizational strategies (work design, leadership, participation) within BGM. Include German and English literature relevant to occupational health management. Exclude: generic public health BGM discussions without stress or mental health components, and clinical treatment studies outside workplace program context.

research_data.desc: Data from workplace health management programs and evaluations: company program data, pre/post intervention measurements, quasi‑experimental and randomized evaluations, and implementation/process datasets focused on stress outcomes.
research_data.narr: Include: program evaluation datasets measuring stress or psychosocial work factors before and after BGM interventions, participation and uptake data, organizational-level indicators (sick leave, productivity) linked to BGM, process evaluation data (implementation fidelity, barriers), and cost data for BGM initiatives. Exclude: datasets from health promotion programs that do not measure stress or psychosocial outcomes and datasets from clinical settings divorced from workplace management strategies.

variables.desc: Program and outcome variables relevant to BGM addressing stress: intervention components, participation, organizational factors, and employee stress and health outcomes.
variables.narr: Include: intervention descriptors (type, duration, target level: individual/organizational), participation rates, measures of perceived stress, job demands/resources, burnout, absenteeism, presenteeism, job satisfaction, productivity metrics, implementation fidelity, costs, and contextual workplace variables (size, sector). Exclude: variables unrelated to workplace health management or lacking linkage to stress/mental health outcomes.

instruments_tools.desc: Assessment tools, survey instruments and program materials used in BGM to assess and intervene on stress and psychosocial working conditions.
instruments_tools.narr: Include: organizational assessment tools (COPSOQ for workplace psychosocial risks, HSE Management Standards Indicator Tool, ERI/JCQ adaptations for organizational surveys), screening tools for employee stress/burnout (PSS, MBI, CBI), program manuals and intervention toolkits for workplace stress management, process evaluation toolkits, and economic evaluation templates used in BGM. Exclude: clinical therapeutic tools not adapted for workplace program delivery or tools lacking relevance for organizational health management.

publication.desc: Scholarly publications (articles, reports, books, theses) in the social sciences on stress at the workplace, including causes, consequences, interventions, and policy implications; emphasis on German-speaking contexts is acceptable but not required.
publication.narr: Relevant publications are empirical studies, theoretical articles, reviews, and policy reports that focus on psychosocial stressors, job strain, work-related stress, burnout, occupational health, and organizational interventions in workplace settings. Included are studies addressing measurement, prevalence, risk factors (e.g., demands, control, effort-reward imbalance, social support), outcomes (mental health, sickness absence, performance), and evaluations of workplace stress reduction programs. Prefer publications in social science disciplines (occupational psychology, sociology, public health, ergonomics). Exclude papers that use the term 'stress' in non-psychosocial senses (e.g., mechanical stress, chemical stress) unless linked to workers' psychosocial health. Include German-language studies ('Arbeitsplatz') and international work if directly about workplace stress.

research_data.desc: Datasets and survey data measuring work-related stress, workplace conditions, and occupational health outcomes, especially those with German samples or workplace-level measures.
research_data.narr: Include cross-sectional and longitudinal datasets, cohort studies, employee surveys, organizational audits, and administrative data that contain variables on job demands, control, effort-reward imbalance, social support, burnout, sickness absence, and related health or performance outcomes. Examples: national working conditions surveys, enterprise surveys, panel studies with employment modules. Exclude datasets that only record physical/chemical exposures without psychosocial or health measures, and datasets unrelated to employment or workplace context.

variables.desc: Variables that capture workplace psychosocial stress and related constructs: perceived stress, job demands, job control, effort-reward imbalance, social support, burnout, absenteeism, presenteeism, and physiological stress markers when linked to workplace exposure.
variables.narr: Relevant variables include single-item and scale measures of perceived work stress, job strain indices (demand-control), effort-reward imbalance scores, social support at work, leadership quality, workload, time pressure, emotional demands, role conflict, role ambiguity, burnout (emotional exhaustion, depersonalization), sickness absence records, self-rated health, and validated physiological indicators (e.g., cortisol) only when measured in workplace studies. Exclude variables that refer to non-work stressors without workplace linkage or to unrelated technical meanings of 'stress.'

instruments_tools.desc: Validated questionnaires, scales, and assessment tools used to measure workplace stress and psychosocial work environment (e.g., COPSOQ, JCQ, ERI, MBI, PSS).
instruments_tools.narr: Include instruments and protocols for assessing job demands-control-support (Job Content Questionnaire, Karasek), Effort-Reward Imbalance questionnaire, Copenhagen Psychosocial Questionnaire (COPSOQ), Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI), Perceived Stress Scale (PSS) when applied to work context, organizational climate surveys, work design checklists, interview guides, and workplace risk assessment tools. Also include translation/adaptation studies and technical documentation. Exclude instruments unrelated to psychosocial workplace measurement or those solely biomedical without workplace linkage.

publication.desc: Publications on stress at the workplace (explicit phrasing 'stress am Arbeitsplatz'), emphasizing studies of causes, measurement, outcomes, and interventions within occupational and organizational settings.
publication.narr: Include empirical articles, literature reviews, practice-oriented reports, and policy briefs analyzing work-related stress, psychosocial hazards at work, mental health outcomes from workplace strain, and evaluations of workplace interventions. Studies in German or explicitly using the phrase 'am Arbeitsplatz' are especially relevant, but international comparable studies are also included. Exclude materials where 'stress' is used in unrelated domains (e.g., material stress) or where workplace context is absent.

research_data.desc: Empirical datasets and survey collections that document stress experienced at the workplace, including employee surveys, occupational health registries, and company-level assessments.
research_data.narr: Relevant data resources are those that provide measures of stress specifically 'at the workplace' such as workplace surveys, occupational cohort datasets, administrative records of work-related absenteeism or disability, and intervention trial data collected in work settings. Include datasets with contextual workplace items (e.g., department, occupation, shift work). Exclude datasets that do not differentiate workplace stress from other stress domains.

variables.desc: Workplace-specific stress variables: perceived stress at work, work demands, control/autonomy at work, job insecurity, work–family conflict, burnout dimensions tied to job role.
variables.narr: Include variables explicitly referencing stress at work or workplace conditions (e.g., 'stress am Arbeitsplatz', 'Arbeitsbelastung'), measures of psychosocial work factors (demands, control, support), job insecurity, work hours, shift patterns, and occupational role stressors. Also include outcome variables like work-related mental health diagnoses, absence due to workplace stress, and productivity indicators linked to stress. Exclude generic life-stress measures not tied to the workplace.

instruments_tools.desc: Tools for assessing workplace-specific stressors and outcomes, including workplace surveys, psychosocial risk assessment tools, and validated scales adapted for workplace phrasing.
instruments_tools.narr: Include instruments explicitly used to measure 'stress at the workplace' such as workplace versions/translations of COPSOQ, Job Content Questionnaire, Effort-Reward Imbalance, MBI for occupational burnout, the Work Ability Index, company psychosocial risk assessment protocols, and intervention toolkits. Include user manuals, validation studies, and translated/adapted versions for German workplaces. Exclude tools that measure stress only in non-work contexts.

publication.desc: Broad social-science publications about stress, including psychological, social, occupational, and public-health perspectives on perceived stress, coping, and outcomes.
publication.narr: Include empirical research, reviews, theoretical work, and policy analyses on human stress (psychological stress, chronic stress, acute stress responses), coping mechanisms, social determinants of stress, mental health consequences, and interventions. Accept studies from psychology, sociology, public health, epidemiology, and occupational health that conceptualize and measure stress. Exclude material using 'stress' in purely physical sciences contexts (e.g., mechanical stress in materials) unless explicitly linked to human or social consequences.

research_data.desc: Datasets that capture measures of stress or stress-related constructs across populations—survey data, cohort studies, experimental data, and psychophysiological datasets.
research_data.narr: Include national and international surveys with stress measures (e.g., PSS items), longitudinal cohorts tracking stress and health outcomes, laboratory/experimental datasets on stress responses, and datasets combining biomarkers (cortisol, heart rate variability) with psychosocial measures. Exclude datasets where 'stress' is absent as a measured construct or used in unrelated technical contexts.

variables.desc: Core variables capturing perceived stress, life-event stressors, chronic stress, coping, social support, and physiological stress indicators (e.g., cortisol).
variables.narr: Include scale and item-level measures of perceived stress (Perceived Stress Scale), number and severity of life events, chronic strain indices, coping strategies, social network/support measures, anxiety/depression symptoms as stress outcomes, and biomarkers of stress response when collected in human studies. Exclude environmental or mechanical stress indicators not related to human psychosocial experience.

instruments_tools.desc: Validated instruments for measuring stress and related constructs (PSS, life-events checklists, Trier Social Stress Test protocols, biomarker sampling protocols), along with coding schemes and manuals.
instruments_tools.narr: Include psychometric scales (Perceived Stress Scale, Holmes-Rahe Life Events Scale), structured interview guides, experimental stress induction protocols (e.g., Trier Social Stress Test), biomarker collection and assay protocols for cortisol and other stress hormones, and standardized coping/support measures. Include documentation, validation studies, and translations. Exclude instruments irrelevant to human stress measurement or focused on non-social science domains.

publication.desc: Publications in social sciences addressing sustainability concepts, sustainable development, environmental attitudes and behaviors, corporate/social policy sustainability, and measurement of sustainability-related outcomes.
publication.narr: Include empirical studies, theoretical analyses, reviews, and policy papers on sustainability as it pertains to environmental, social, and economic dimensions; sustainable consumption; attitudes and behaviors toward sustainability; organizational sustainability practices; and the social implications of sustainability transitions. Studies on measurement and indicators of sustainability (including SDG-related research) are relevant. Exclude purely technical engineering studies of sustainable technologies that lack social science analysis unless they address social adoption, policy, or behavioral aspects.

research_data.desc: Datasets that measure sustainability-related attitudes, behaviors, practices, and indicators—including surveys (e.g., Eurobarometer, ISSP modules), consumption panels, corporate sustainability datasets, and environmental indicators linked to social data.
research_data.narr: Include cross-national and national surveys with sustainability items, datasets on household or firm-level sustainable practices (energy use, recycling, transport choices), longitudinal studies of environmental behavior change, and datasets linking social variables to environmental indicators. Also include data on SDG indicators where social variables are present. Exclude datasets solely focused on technical environmental measurements without social/behavioral variables.

variables.desc: Variables capturing sustainability attitudes, environmental concern, pro-environmental behaviors, sustainable consumption, corporate social responsibility indicators, and policy support for sustainability measures.
variables.narr: Relevant variables include measures of environmental concern (e.g., NEP scale), frequency of pro-environmental actions (recycling, public transport use), willingness to pay for green products, sustainability-related values and norms, organizational sustainability practices, and indicators tied to sustainability goals (energy consumption, carbon footprint proxies) when linked to social units. Exclude technical environmental metrics lacking social context.

instruments_tools.desc: Surveys, scales, and measurement tools for sustainability-related constructs (NEP scale, environmental behavior inventories, corporate sustainability assessment tools, SDG indicator toolkits).
instruments_tools.narr: Include validated questionnaires for environmental attitudes (New Ecological Paradigm), behavioral inventories, household energy use survey modules, corporate sustainability reporting standards and assessment instruments, measurement protocols for sustainable consumption studies, and toolkits for operationalizing SDG indicators in social research. Also include manuals and validation studies. Exclude technical measurement tools unrelated to social-science assessment of sustainability.

publication.desc: Social-science publications on trust — interpersonal, generalized, institutional, political/trust in organizations — including causes, consequences, and measurement.
publication.narr: Include empirical research, theoretical treatments, reviews, and policy analyses examining the formation and effects of trust at individual, group, organizational, and societal levels. Topics include generalized social trust, political/institutional trust, trust in institutions and markets, trust dynamics in organizations, and the role of trust in cooperation and social capital. Include cross-national comparisons and survey-based studies (e.g., WVS, ESS, ISSP). Exclude non-social uses of 'trust' (e.g., cryptographic trust models) unless they have social-science relevance.

research_data.desc: Datasets containing trust measures (e.g., World Values Survey, European Social Survey, ISSP, national surveys) and experimental datasets from trust games and lab/field experiments.
research_data.narr: Include large-scale surveys with trust items (generalized trust question, confidence in institutions), panel datasets tracking trust over time, datasets from behavioral experiments (trust games, investment games), and administrative data linked to trust-related outcomes. Also include datasets measuring organizational or institutional trust. Exclude datasets where 'trust' is absent or used in unrelated technical contexts.

variables.desc: Variables measuring types of trust: generalized social trust, interpersonal trust, institutional/political trust, trust in specific actors (government, judiciary, media), and related constructs (social capital, confidence, reciprocity).
variables.narr: Include single-item measures (e.g., 'Generally speaking, would you say that most people can be trusted?') and multi-item scales assessing interpersonal trust, institutional confidence, and trustworthiness perceptions. Also include variables on trust behaviors from experiments, measures of reciprocity, and indicators of social capital. Exclude variables using 'trust' in technical/non-social contexts.

instruments_tools.desc: Survey questions, validated scales, and experimental protocols used to measure trust (e.g., standard WVS/ESS trust items, Rotter Interpersonal Trust Scale, trust game designs).
instruments_tools.narr: Include widely used survey items (WVS/ESS/ISSP trust questions), psychometric trust scales (Rotter, Yamagishi), instruments for measuring institutional trust, experimental trust-game protocols and coding schemes, and manuals documenting administration and validation. Also include translated/adapted versions and methodological studies on measurement equivalence. Exclude technical security/trust models without social-science measurement focus.

publication.desc: Publications (articles, reports, books) that analyze environmental awareness, attitudes, knowledge, and self‑reported pro‑environmental behavior among the German population or German subpopulations.
publication.narr: Include empirical and theoretical works whose primary focus is public environmental awareness in Germany (national surveys, regional studies, longitudinal analyses, comparative studies that report German results separately). Relevant topics: environmental attitudes, perceived environmental problems, environmental knowledge, risk perceptions, value orientations linked to environmentalism, and determinants of pro‑environmental behavior in German samples. Exclude purely natural‑science studies of environmental conditions (e.g. pollution measurements) unless they explicitly study public awareness; exclude publications limited to technical mitigation methods, biodiversity/ecology research without social or attitudinal components, and works that treat Germany only incidentally without extractable German findings.

research_data.desc: Survey and observational datasets that contain measures of environmental awareness, attitudes, beliefs, knowledge or self‑reported environmental behaviour for respondents in Germany.
research_data.narr: Include datasets with German national or subnational samples (or pooled/comparative surveys with identifiable German cases) that include items on environmental concern, climate change belief, environmental knowledge tests, willingness to pay for environmental goods, recycling/consumption behaviours, or related items (e.g. SOEP modules, ALLBUS, ISSP Environment, Eurobarometer subsets, country slices of ESS). Also include longitudinal panels with repeated measures of environmental awareness in Germany. Exclude raw environmental monitoring or ecological sensor data that do not measure human attitudes or behaviour, and datasets with no identifiable German respondents.

variables.desc: Variable‑level metadata that operationalize environmental awareness and related constructs among individuals in Germany.
variables.narr: Include variable names, labels and item wording that capture environmental concern/awareness (e.g. 'environmental concern', 'climate change belief', 'environmental knowledge score', 'willingness to pay', 'recycling frequency', 'frequency of pro‑environmental actions') in German datasets or translations. Also include sociodemographic covariates used in analyses of awareness (age, education, region). Exclude variables that only measure environmental parameters (e.g. pollutant concentrations) or macro‑level policy indicators that do not reflect individual awareness.

instruments_tools.desc: Validated survey instruments, question batteries, scales and measurement protocols used to assess environmental awareness, attitudes and behaviour in German contexts.
instruments_tools.narr: Include German versions and translations of established scales (e.g. New Ecological Paradigm (NEP) scale German adaptation), ISSP/Eurobarometer/ESS question modules on environment, environmental knowledge tests, survey question batteries, coding manuals for constructing composite indices of environmental awareness, and interviewer guidelines used in German surveys. Exclude technical environmental measurement tools (lab or sensor protocols) and instruments not intended to measure human attitudes or behaviour.

publication.desc: Publications examining environmental protection as policy, practice, public support, governance, or collective action, including studies in Germany and comparative analyses that address environmental protection measures.
publication.narr: Include works that focus on environmental protection policies and instruments (regulation, protected areas, conservation programs), public attitudes and support for protection measures, activism and NGO roles in environmental protection, policy evaluation, and social/scientific analyses of protective interventions. Relevant geographic scope includes Germany specifically and comparative studies with extractable findings on environmental protection. Exclude purely technical engineering studies of remediation techniques unless they include social/policy evaluation; exclude basic ecological research that does not address protection policy or societal dimensions.

research_data.desc: Datasets and data collections related to environmental protection: policy indicators, public opinion on protection measures, protected area statistics, emissions mitigation data and data on participation in environmental protection activities.
research_data.narr: Include datasets documenting environmental policy instruments and outcomes (protected areas, Natura 2000 sites, emissions by sector), survey data on public support for environmental protection and participation in conservation (national surveys, Eurobarometer, ISSP, ESS, NGO membership data), and administrative datasets on regulatory compliance or program uptake. Exclude raw ecological monitoring datasets that do not relate to protection policy or human responses, and datasets unrelated to protection (e.g. purely biodiversity inventories without protection context).

variables.desc: Variables that measure dimensions of environmental protection, including policy outputs, institutional measures, and individual attitudes or behaviours supporting protection.
variables.narr: Include variables such as extent of protected areas, number of conservation programs, emissions reductions, presence/strength of specific environmental regulations, individual survey items on support for environmental protection, membership in environmental organizations, participation in conservation activities, and willingness‑to‑pay for protection. Exclude variables that solely measure ecological conditions without linkage to protection policy or societal engagement.

instruments_tools.desc: Evaluation frameworks, survey modules, indices and measurement tools used to assess environmental protection policies, programs and public support.
instruments_tools.narr: Include policy evaluation frameworks, environmental performance indices (EPI, national equivalents), survey question batteries on support for protection measures, instruments for measuring conservation behaviour, NGO monitoring tools, and manuals for counting/assessing protected areas. Exclude laboratory or field instruments used exclusively for ecological sampling or environmental chemistry that do not assess protection policy or social responses.

publication.desc: Scholarly and policy publications analyzing social and economic inequality (income, wealth, education, health, opportunity) including causes, consequences, trends and redistribution, with relevance to Germany or broader comparative contexts.
publication.narr: Include empirical studies, reviews, and policy analyses that examine distributional outcomes (income/wealth inequality, poverty, social stratification, health and educational disparities), measurement and decomposition of inequality, and policy responses. Both Germany‑specific and comparative works are relevant if they present disaggregated or generalizable findings about inequality. Exclude publications that address inequality only metaphorically (e.g. literary uses) or that focus exclusively on non‑distributional phenomena (e.g. measurement error papers without application to inequality).

research_data.desc: Microdata and aggregated datasets used to measure socioeconomic inequality: household surveys, administrative tax and social security data, wealth surveys and comparative datasets with inequality indicators.
research_data.narr: Include SOEP, EU‑SILC, German Income and Expenditure Survey, national tax/administrative microdata, household wealth surveys, LIS, OECD distributional datasets, and other data sources that allow analysis of income/wealth/consumption distributions, poverty rates and intergenerational mobility. Datasets should provide variables needed for inequality measurement (income components, household composition, sampling weights). Exclude datasets that do not permit distributional analysis (e.g. purely qualitative case studies without measurable economic indicators).

variables.desc: Variable metadata relevant to measuring inequality: income and wealth components, equivalence scales, poverty indicators, and socioeconomic status markers.
variables.narr: Include variables such as gross/net household income, individual earnings, capital income, household wealth, consumption expenditures, equivalized disposable income, income percentiles/deciles, Gini/Theil coefficients, poverty thresholds, educational attainment, occupational class, and parental background indicators used in mobility and inequality research. Exclude variables unrelated to distributional analyses (e.g. purely clinical health measures without population distribution context) unless explicitly linked to inequality outcomes.

instruments_tools.desc: Methods, indices, survey modules and computational tools used to measure and analyze inequality and social stratification.
instruments_tools.narr: Include descriptions of equivalence scales (OECD), measurement and decomposition methods (Gini, Theil, Atkinson, quantile regression), survey question modules for income and wealth collection, coding schemes for occupation/class (ISCO, EGP), instruments for measuring social mobility, and software codebooks or scripts commonly used for inequality analysis. Exclude tools unrelated to distributional measurement (e.g. laboratory instruments).

publication.desc: Research publications on non‑conventional political participation: protests, demonstrations, civil disobedience, petitions, boycotts, online activism and other forms of political engagement outside voting and party membership.
publication.narr: Include empirical studies, theoretical treatments and comparative analyses that focus specifically on unconventional political participation (frequency, causes, effects, demographic correlates, mobilization processes), especially those including German cases or cross‑national comparisons with extractable results. Exclude works that focus solely on conventional participation (voting, party membership) unless they explicitly analyze or contrast unconventional forms; exclude purely historical accounts without analysis of participation patterns unless they inform contemporary forms.

research_data.desc: Datasets that measure participation in protests, signing petitions, boycotting, online political actions, and other non‑electoral forms of political engagement.
research_data.narr: Include survey sources with items on unconventional participation (e.g. Eurobarometer, ESS items on protest and petitioning, ALLBUS modules, GESIS protest/activism modules), event datasets capturing protests/demonstrations (national protest event data, project event data for Germany), and digital trace datasets from petition platforms or social media when they document non‑conventional participation. Exclude datasets limited to electoral turnout or party membership if they do not include unconventional participation measures.

variables.desc: Variables capturing individual engagement in unconventional political actions and related motivations or frequencies.
variables.narr: Include variables such as participation in demonstrations/protests, signing petitions, contacting politicians, online political petitions/sharing, boycotts, occupying or direct action, frequency of such activities, motivations for participation, and perceived efficacy. Also include related measures (political efficacy, trust, media use) when used to explain unconventional participation. Exclude variables that only measure traditional electoral participation unless paired with unconventional participation items.

instruments_tools.desc: Question batteries, scales, coding manuals and event‑coding protocols used to measure or classify unconventional political participation.
instruments_tools.narr: Include survey question wordings for protest and petition items, validated scales for political activism, coding schemes for event data (protest event coding protocols), instrument guides for collecting online activism data, and interviewer instructions for sensitive political behaviour questions. Exclude instruments that only measure conventional political behaviour (voting intention modules) or technical tools unrelated to measuring political participation.

publication.desc: Publications investigating attributions of responsibility for environmental problems (who is responsible: individuals, governments, industry, international actors), including normative and empirical analyses of responsibility beliefs, moral obligations and policy preferences.
publication.narr: Include empirical surveys, experimental studies, normative discussions and policy analyses that examine how responsibility for environmental problems is perceived and how these attributions relate to support for policies, behaviour change, or blame attribution. Relevant contexts include Germany and comparative studies with extractable national results. Exclude technical environmental science papers that do not address social perceptions of responsibility, and philosophical treatises that do not engage empirical measurement when empirical scope is required.

research_data.desc: Datasets containing survey items or experimental measures about perceived responsibility for environmental degradation, climate change and related problems, specifying agents held responsible.
research_data.narr: Include survey modules (ISSP Environment, Eurobarometer, ESS slices, national surveys) that ask respondents whether individuals, governments, corporations, or other actors are responsible for environmental problems and about who should act. Also include experimental datasets testing causal attributions or interventions to shift responsibility perceptions. Exclude datasets that only measure ecological conditions without data on human attributions or normative beliefs.

variables.desc: Variables that operationalize attribution of responsibility for environmental problems (e.g. items identifying responsible actors, willingness to accept responsibility, perceived effectiveness of actors).
variables.narr: Include item‑level variables such as 'who is most responsible for climate change' (individuals/industry/government), scales of perceived government/industry responsibility, measures of personal responsibility or guilt, willingness to pay or change behaviour, and perceived attribution of blame. Also include moderator variables commonly used in such analyses (political ideology, trust, environmental values). Exclude variables that do not capture attribution or normative responsibility (e.g. objective pollution levels).

instruments_tools.desc: Survey question batteries, vignette instruments, experimental protocols and coding schemes designed to measure attribution of responsibility and related normative attitudes about environmental problems.
instruments_tools.narr: Include validated question wordings and vignettes used to elicit responsibility attributions (e.g. forced‑choice responsibility items, Likert scales for perceived actor responsibility), experimental designs manipulating responsibility framing, coding manuals for classifying open‑ended responsibility attributions, and instruments that measure moral norms and willingness to act. Exclude ecological measurement tools and technical instruments unrelated to measuring social attributions of responsibility.

publication.desc: Publications addressing the concept of trust (vertrauen) in social sciences: theoretical treatments, empirical studies, literature reviews and meta-analyses that explicitly analyze trust as an outcome, predictor, or construct.
publication.narr: Include peer‑reviewed articles, book chapters, conference papers and research reports in sociology, political science, psychology, economics and communication that explicitly focus on trust (vertrauen). Relevant works discuss interpersonal trust, generalized social trust, institutional trust, scales and measurement of trust, antecedents and consequences of trust, cross‑national comparisons, longitudinal analyses and theoretical frameworks. Exclude works that use the word 'trust' only in passing, legal/financial uses of the term 'trust' (e.g., trust funds, legal trust instruments) without social‑scientific treatment, personal names or organizational names containing 'Trust', and publications where 'vertrauen' is not a primary subject (e.g., studies that list 'trust' as one of many unrelated keywords without analysis).

research_data.desc: Datasets and survey data that contain measures of trust (vertrauen): cross‑national surveys, panels, experiments and administrative datasets with trust items or trust behavior measures.
research_data.narr: Include raw and processed datasets, codebooks and variable documentation from large surveys (e.g., ESS, World Values Survey, Eurobarometer, GESIS data collections), national surveys and panel studies with items measuring interpersonal or institutional trust, experimental datasets (trust games, behavioral measures), and scales data where 'vertrauen' items are present. Metadata and documentation enabling reuse (variable descriptions, sampling, weighting) should be included. Exclude datasets that do not contain explicit trust measures (no self‑report or behavioral trust indicators), data about legal trusts or financial instruments, or datasets lacking sufficient documentation to identify trust variables.

variables.desc: Variables operationalizing trust (vertrauen): single‑item and multi‑item measures, indices, and behavioral indicators capturing interpersonal, generalized or institutional trust.
variables.narr: Include variables labelled as trust, confidence, reliability, or trustworthiness that measure interpersonal trust (e.g., 'Generally speaking, would you say that most people can be trusted?'), institutional trust (trust in government, courts, police), and composite trust indices. Include psychometric details (scale range, item wording, reverse coding) and derived indicators (factor scores). Also include behavioral trust measures (amount sent in a trust game). Exclude variables unrelated to social trust such as legal/financial trust ownership fields, or items measuring unrelated constructs (e.g., mere familiarity or satisfaction) unless explicitly validated as trust measures.

instruments_tools.desc: Validated instruments and methods for measuring trust (vertrauen): questionnaires, psychometric scales, experimental paradigms and coding schemes used to assess trust.
instruments_tools.narr: Include established scales and instruments such as the General Social Survey/WVS single trust item, Rotter Interpersonal Trust Scale, Yamagishi General Trust Scale, institutional trust batteries used in ESS/WVS, and experimental tools such as the Trust Game (binary and continuous versions) and repeated‑trust paradigms. Also include validated multi‑item scales for dimensions of trust (competence/benevolence/integrity) and translation/adaptation documentation for German 'vertrauen' measures. Exclude ad hoc or single‑item measures with no documentation, instruments aimed at legal/financial trust instruments, and tools unrelated to measuring social or institutional trust.

publication.desc: Publications on trust in technology (vertrauen in technologie): empirical and theoretical work examining users' trust in technologies, automation, AI, internet services and technical systems.
publication.narr: Include peer‑reviewed studies, book chapters and reports that explicitly investigate trust in technical systems — e.g., automation, algorithms, artificial intelligence, social media platforms, online services, medical devices, and robots. Relevant topics are antecedents and consequences of trust in technology, measurement of trust in automation, trust calibration, human–machine interaction, and cross‑cultural comparisons of technological trust. Exclude publications that discuss technology acceptance or adoption without reference to trust or trust constructs, legal/contractual trust instruments, or studies where technology is only background context and trust is not analyzed.

research_data.desc: Datasets containing measures of trust in technology: surveys, experiments, log data and field studies capturing users' trust in specific technologies or automation.
research_data.narr: Include data from lab and field experiments on human‑automation trust, survey datasets with trust‑in‑technology items (e.g., trust in online platforms, AI systems), usability studies with trust ratings, and longitudinal/adaptive datasets measuring changes in trust after exposure to technology. Also include anonymized interaction logs that are used to infer trust (e.g., reliance actions). Exclude datasets without explicit trust measures, datasets only about technology usage or acceptance where trust is not measured, and proprietary datasets lacking documentation on trust variables.

variables.desc: Variables capturing trust in technology: self‑reported trust scores, dimension scores (reliability, predictability, safety), behavioral reliance measures and indices specific to technical domains.
variables.narr: Include variables labeled as trust in automation/AI/robots/platforms, items measuring perceived reliability, predictability, perceived risk, willingness to rely, and composite trust scales (e.g., McKnight et al. online trust adapted for technology).
