Include behavioral measures (frequency of automation override, amount entrusted to an automated decision) and context‑specific trust variables (e.g., trust in medical devices vs. social media). Exclude generic usage variables (e.g., login frequency) unless accompanied by validated trust items, and variables that measure only acceptance without trust content.

instruments_tools.desc: Instruments and experimental tools for measuring trust in technology: validated questionnaires, trust in automation scales and behavioral paradigms tailored to human–technology interaction.
instruments_tools.narr: Include established instruments such as Jian, Bisantz and Drury's Trust in Automation scale, the Human–Robot Interaction trust questionnaires, McKnight et al.'s online trust scales adapted for technology, trust calibration protocols, and behavioral paradigms (trust game variants adapted for automation, reliance/override tasks, simulated driving trust tasks). Also include usability testing protocols and measurement instruments capturing perceived competence, benevolence and integrity of technical systems. Exclude instruments that measure only technology acceptance (TAM) unless accompanied by validated trust subscales, and tools that do not produce trust‑related metrics.

publication.desc: Publications about political trust (vertrauen in politik): studies on trust in political institutions, political actors, democratic legitimacy and citizen confidence in governance.
publication.narr: Include scholarly articles, books and reports that explicitly analyze trust in politics — trust in government, parliament, political parties, politicians, courts, and public administration. Relevant themes: determinants of political trust, consequences for participation and compliance, cross‑national and longitudinal analyses, crisis effects on political trust, and measurement issues in political trust research. Exclude works focused on trust in non‑political institutions (unless compared to political institutions) and studies mentioning 'political' only peripherally without measuring political trust.

research_data.desc: Datasets measuring political trust: national and international surveys, panel data, election studies and experimental datasets containing items on trust in political actors and institutions.
research_data.narr: Include datasets such as ESS, European Social Survey, Eurobarometer, Comparative Study of Electoral Systems, national election studies and longitudinal panels that include items on trust in government, parliament, parties, and politicians. Include experimental datasets testing messaging effects on political trust and administrative data used to validate trust measures. Exclude datasets without explicit political trust items or that measure political attitudes only indirectly without trust constructs.

variables.desc: Variables operationalizing trust in politics: single‑item and multi‑item measures of confidence in government, trust in institutions and trust in politicians, and derived indices of political trust.
variables.narr: Include variables labeled 'trust in government', 'confidence in parliament', 'trust in parties', and composite political trust indices, with documentation of question wording, response scales and any recoding. Also include measures of institutional performance perceptions when explicitly used to operationalize political trust. Exclude variables unrelated to political trust (e.g., party preference, vote intention) unless accompanied by validated trust measures and exclude vague satisfaction items unless theoretically linked to trust and documented as such.

instruments_tools.desc: Measurement instruments and tools for political trust: survey items, validated political trust scales, experimental vignettes and coding schemes used to assess trust in political actors and institutions.
instruments_tools.narr: Include standard survey items used in ESS/Eurobarometer/WVS for political trust, multi‑item trust batteries for institutions, validated questionnaires measuring trust and legitimacy, vignette experiments manipulating governmental performance, and coding manuals for qualitative assessment of trust in political texts. Also include psychometric evaluations and translations into German. Exclude instruments that only measure political knowledge or partisanship without trust constructs, and tools aimed solely at civic education rather than measurement.

publication.desc: Publications on work–life balance: empirical and theoretical literature examining the balance between paid work and non‑work life, its determinants, outcomes and interventions.
publication.narr: Include peer‑reviewed articles, books, reports and policy papers that explicitly address work–life balance, work‑family conflict/facilitation, flexible work arrangements, well‑being, occupational health, organizational practices, gender differences in work–life balance, and evaluations of interventions (e.g., parental leave, telework). Accept cross‑sectional, longitudinal and experimental studies as well as systematic reviews and meta‑analyses. Exclude papers that use the phrase only tangentially, studies exclusively about economic productivity without reference to work–life balance, and purely technical descriptions of workplace systems with no human outcomes.

research_data.desc: Datasets related to work–life balance: surveys, panel studies, organizational datasets and intervention trial data containing measures of work–life balance, work–family conflict, time use and related outcomes.
research_data.narr: Include national time‑use studies, labour force surveys with work–life balance items, panel datasets (e.g., German Socio‑Economic Panel) containing work–family conflict/facilitation measures, employer survey data on flexible work policies, and evaluation datasets from workplace interventions. Include codebooks and variable descriptions for work hours, caregiving responsibilities, flexibility and well‑being indicators. Exclude datasets lacking any measures of work–life balance or time use, and administrative payroll datasets without relevant survey components.

variables.desc: Variables capturing work–life balance: self‑reported balance/conflict/facilitation items, time‑use measures, working hours, flexible working arrangements and well‑being indicators linked to balance.
variables.narr: Include items such as 'Work–life balance' self‑ratings, work‑family conflict scales (time‑based, strain‑based, behavior‑based), family‑to‑work facilitation, number of weekly work hours, commuting time, telework frequency, caregiving hours, and related outcomes (stress, job satisfaction, health). Include coding details (units, scales, reversals) and derived indices. Exclude variables that only record employment status with no measures of time allocation or perceived balance, and variables measuring organizational performance without employee work–life outcomes.

instruments_tools.desc: Instruments and tools for assessing work–life balance: validated questionnaires, time‑use diaries, survey modules and evaluation tools for workplace policies.
instruments_tools.narr: Include validated scales such as the Work–Family Conflict Scale (Netemeyer et al.), Work–Family Enrichment measures, time‑use diary protocols, standardized survey modules used in Eurofound or national labour surveys, and evaluation instruments for flexible working interventions. Also include software/code for analyzing time‑use data and protocols for qualitative interviews about work–life balance. Exclude informal single‑item measures without validation unless well documented, and HR administrative tools that do not measure employee perceptions or time allocation.

publication.desc: Publications related to 'work' broadly: scholarly literature on work, employment, occupations, labour markets, job quality, and workplace processes within social sciences.
publication.narr: Include academic articles, books and reports that explicitly study aspects of work and employment: job characteristics, labour market participation, occupational stratification, employment relationships, workplace wellbeing, skills and training, informal work and unpaid work. Also include interdisciplinary treatments (sociology, economics, psychology, industrial relations). Exclude uses of 'work' in non‑employment contexts without relevance (e.g., 'artwork', scientific 'work' as a synonym for 'study' with no employment focus) and documents where 'work' appears only incidentally.

research_data.desc: Datasets on work and employment: labour force surveys, panel studies, employer surveys, occupational classifications and administrative employment records.
research_data.narr: Include national labour force surveys, household panels (e.g., SOEP, EU‑LFS, ILO statistics), employer/establishment surveys, occupational skill and wages datasets, time‑use surveys for unpaid work, and administrative records with employment spells. Datasets should have variables on employment status, occupation, working hours, wages, job tenure and job quality. Exclude datasets that do not concern work or employment (e.g., purely clinical trials) and those lacking documentation on employment variables.

variables.desc: Variables describing work: employment status, occupation, working hours, wages/income, contract type, job tenure, job satisfaction and related job quality indicators.
variables.narr: Include variables such as employment/unemployment status, full/part‑time indicator, ISCO/ISCO‑08 occupation codes, sector, hourly/weekly wages, contract type (temporary/permanent), working hours, shift work indicator, job tenure, occupational hazards, job satisfaction, and measures of job autonomy. Provide variable labels, coding schemes and units. Exclude variables that do not pertain to work (e.g., merely sector tags without clarity) or social variables unrelated to employment.

instruments_tools.desc: Instruments and tools for measuring work and employment: survey modules, occupational classification systems, job quality indices, time‑use instruments and experimental/qualitative protocols.
instruments_tools.narr: Include standardized instruments like labour force survey questionnaires, ISCO occupation coding manuals, job content questionnaires (Karasek Job Content Questionnaire), OECD job quality indices, time‑use diary methodologies, employer survey instruments, and qualitative interview guides for workplaces. Also include tools for wage and occupational coding and software for analysing employment trajectories. Exclude instruments that measure unrelated constructs (e.g., purely technical productivity metrics without work context) or proprietary HR tools without methodological documentation.

publication.desc: Scholarly publications (articles, book chapters, dissertations, reviews) that study work–family conflict (WFC) or family–work conflict (FWC), including theoretical models, antecedents, consequences, and interventions.
publication.narr: Relevant publications: empirical and theoretical studies explicitly addressing work–family conflict or family–work conflict; cross-sectional, longitudinal, and intervention studies examining predictors (e.g., job demands, working hours, childcare arrangements), outcomes (e.g., job satisfaction, mental health, turnover intentions), measurement and scale validation; meta-analyses and systematic reviews on WFC/FWC; cross-cultural comparisons. Exclude: works that only mention work or family topics without explicit measurement or discussion of conflict between domains; organizational-level reports without individual-level WFC measures; purely economic or macro policy papers that do not address individual work–family conflict.

research_data.desc: Individual-level datasets and survey studies that include measures of work–family conflict or family–work conflict, plus related covariates (work hours, job characteristics, family structure, wellbeing).
research_data.narr: Relevant datasets: national and international surveys or panel studies that include validated WFC/FWC items or multi-item scales (e.g., items from Netemeyer, Carlson, Frone), time-use diaries linked to family and work demands, workplace surveys with family conflict modules, longitudinal panels tracking work and family outcomes. Include datasets with variables for work schedules, childcare, spousal employment, health and wellbeing to permit analysis of antecedents and consequences. Exclude: aggregate or organizational-level datasets without individual WFC measures; datasets only about macro labor market statistics that lack individual role-conflict variables.

variables.desc: Individual-level variables that measure or relate directly to conflict between work and family roles, plus common antecedents and outcomes.
variables.narr: Relevant variables: direct measures of work–family conflict and family–work conflict (single- or multi-item scales); subdimensions (time-based, strain-based, behavior-based); antecedents such as working hours, shift work, job demands, job control, supervisor support, childcare availability, number/age of children, partner employment; outcomes such as job satisfaction, life satisfaction, burnout, mental health, absenteeism, turnover intentions. Exclude: variables unrelated to role conflict (purely macro indicators, organizational financial metrics) unless linked to individual WFC measures.

instruments_tools.desc: Validated instruments and measurement tools for assessing work–family conflict and related constructs, plus methods for data collection (diaries, scales).
instruments_tools.narr: Relevant instruments: established WFC/FWC scales such as Netemeyer et al. (1996) work–family conflict scale, Carlson et al. (2000) multidimensional WFC scale (time/strain/behavior and directions), Frone’s measures, Greenhaus and Beutell (1985) conceptual measures; time-use diaries capturing overlapping demands; validated translations/adaptations for different languages/countries. Include psychometric validation reports and scoring instructions. Exclude: general stress or wellbeing scales that do not contain items assessing inter-role conflict, and ad-hoc single items without demonstrated validity for WFC unless clearly labeled as WFC measures.

publication.desc: Publications examining conflict between work and non-work life (work–life conflict), including definitions, empirical evidence on causes/consequences, and interventions to improve work–life balance.
publication.narr: Relevant publications: empirical studies, theoretical papers, reviews and policy analyses focused on work–life conflict (synonymous with work–family conflict when non-work includes family and other life domains); studies of antecedents (e.g., boundary management, technology use), outcomes (wellbeing, productivity), and interventions (flexible work arrangements). Exclude: studies that use the term 'work–life' only in passing without measuring conflict; literature focused solely on leisure or non-conflict aspects of work–life enrichment unless conflict is directly addressed.

research_data.desc: Datasets and survey studies containing measures of work–life conflict or related constructs (e.g., boundary management, work–nonwork interference), plus contextual variables.
research_data.narr: Relevant datasets: national and organizational surveys with work–life or work–nonwork conflict items, time-use studies capturing interference between work and non-work domains, panel data enabling longitudinal analysis of work–life conflict and outcomes. Include data with variables on flexible work practices, technology use for work, caregiving responsibilities, and wellbeing. Exclude: datasets that only measure general work satisfaction or leisure satisfaction without items on interference or conflict between domains.

variables.desc: Variables measuring interference between paid work and other life domains (family, leisure, caregiving) and associated predictors and outcomes.
variables.narr: Relevant variables: work–life conflict and life–work conflict measures, subtypes (time/strain/behavioral interference), boundary control, telework frequency, work hours, work intensity, caregiving responsibilities, social support, job and life satisfaction, stress and health outcomes. Exclude: variables limited to enrichment or positive spillover unless conflict is also measured; purely organizational metrics with no individual-level work–life information.

instruments_tools.desc: Measurement instruments, scales, and data-collection methods for assessing work–life conflict and related constructs (e.g., boundary management).
instruments_tools.narr: Relevant instruments: validated work–life conflict scales (adaptations of Netemeyer, Carlson, Greenhaus and Beutell), boundary management questionnaires, telework and flexible work arrangement modules, time-use diaries and ecological momentary assessment tools capturing work–nonwork interference. Include tool validation studies and translated versions. Exclude: instruments that only assess positive work–life enrichment without items on conflict unless combined with conflict measures.

publication.desc: Publications studying satisfaction with education and vocational training (trainee/apprenticeship satisfaction), including determinants, outcomes (completion, performance), and training quality assessments.
publication.narr: Relevant publications: empirical studies, program evaluations and reviews on satisfaction with vocational education, apprenticeships, and formal training programs; papers on predictors (training quality, instructor support, learning opportunities), consequences (dropout, career trajectories, job satisfaction), and cross-national comparisons of trainee satisfaction. Exclude: general education satisfaction papers that do not address vocational/training context; publications about satisfaction in higher education only unless they specifically address vocational/teacher training contexts.

research_data.desc: Datasets and surveys that include measures of satisfaction with vocational education or apprenticeship training, plus related contextual variables (training firm characteristics, trainer support).
research_data.narr: Relevant datasets: vocational training surveys and panels (e.g., National Educational Panel Study NEPS modules on vocational training, BIBB surveys of apprentices/training firms), datasets with trainee satisfaction items, training evaluation studies, longitudinal data linking training satisfaction to labor-market outcomes. Include data on training content, instructors, wages during training, and completion/dropout. Exclude: datasets that measure only general school satisfaction in primary/secondary education without vocational training focus.

variables.desc: Variables capturing satisfaction with apprenticeship or vocational training and related aspects of the training environment and outcomes.
variables.narr: Relevant variables: overall trainee satisfaction and domain-specific satisfaction (content, supervision, learning environment, peer relations), perceived training quality, instructor competence/support, opportunities for skill use, apprentices’ wage during training, training duration and completion status, career expectations. Exclude: generic job satisfaction variables unrelated to training context or satisfaction measures for unrelated educational levels unless clearly tied to vocational training.

instruments_tools.desc: Survey instruments and evaluation tools designed to measure trainee/apprentice satisfaction and training quality in vocational and apprenticeship settings.
instruments_tools.narr: Relevant instruments: validated trainee satisfaction questionnaires used in vocational education research and program evaluations, standardized training evaluation modules (institutional surveys, BIBB instruments), items/scales measuring supervisor support and learning opportunities in training, interview guides for qualitative evaluations. Include psychometric documentation and translations for German contexts. Exclude: generic satisfaction scales designed for the workplace that do not assess training-specific aspects unless adapted for apprenticeship contexts.

publication.desc: Scholarly works on satisfaction broadly construed (life satisfaction, job satisfaction, domain-specific satisfaction), including theory, measurement, determinants, and consequences.
publication.narr: Relevant publications: empirical and theoretical studies on subjective wellbeing and satisfaction (life satisfaction, job satisfaction, domain satisfactions such as health, income, relationships), scale development and validation (e.g., SWLS), cross-cultural comparisons and longitudinal analyses of satisfaction trajectories. Exclude: papers that use 'satisfaction' only colloquially without measurement or conceptual focus; clinical studies that only report diagnostic outcomes without addressing satisfaction.

research_data.desc: Surveys and panel datasets that include measures of life satisfaction or domain-specific satisfaction (e.g., SOEP, ESS, WVS, Eurobarometer).
research_data.narr: Relevant datasets: large-scale national and international surveys and longitudinal panels with validated satisfaction items (overall life satisfaction, SWLS, job satisfaction items), interviews and experience sampling studies of subjective wellbeing, domain-specific modules linking satisfaction to socio-demographic and contextual variables. Exclude: administrative data lacking subjective satisfaction measures or datasets with only one-off, non-validated satisfaction items unless clearly labeled as measuring satisfaction.

variables.desc: Individual-level variables measuring overall life satisfaction and domain-specific satisfaction (job, health, income, relationships), plus common predictors and outcomes.
variables.narr: Relevant variables: single-item or multi-item measures of life satisfaction (e.g., ladder or 0–10 items), Satisfaction With Life Scale (SWLS) scores, job satisfaction items, domain-specific satisfaction indicators, predictors such as income, health status, employment, social support, and outcomes including mental health, productivity, and longevity. Exclude: objective indicators (income, employment) only as stand-alone without subjective satisfaction measures unless used as predictors of satisfaction.

instruments_tools.desc: Validated instruments and survey items for assessing life and domain-specific satisfaction and methods for experience sampling of satisfaction.
instruments_tools.narr: Relevant instruments: Satisfaction With Life Scale (Diener), single-item life satisfaction measures used in ESS/Eurobarometer/WVS, standardized job satisfaction items, domain-specific satisfaction scales, experience sampling and day reconstruction methods. Include validation studies, translations, and scoring guidance. Exclude: instruments that measure only affect or clinical symptomatology without assessing evaluative satisfaction.

publication.desc: Publications exploring the relationship between satisfaction (life, job, training) and burden/strain (stress, workload, caregiver burden, burnout), including correlational and causal analyses.
publication.narr: Relevant publications: empirical studies and reviews that examine how satisfaction relates to perceived burden, stress, workload, burnout, and caregiving strain across contexts (workplace, education, caregiving); intervention studies aiming to reduce burden and improve satisfaction; theoretical work linking demand–resource models to satisfaction outcomes. Exclude: studies treating satisfaction and burden as unrelated topics or focusing solely on clinical diagnosis without linking to satisfaction.

research_data.desc: Datasets containing measures of both satisfaction and burden/strain (perceived stress, workload, burnout, caregiving burden), enabling analysis of their relationship.
research_data.narr: Relevant datasets: surveys and panels that include validated satisfaction measures (life/job/training) and measures of burden such as Perceived Stress Scale, Maslach Burnout Inventory, Zarit Burden Interview, workload items, health and wellbeing indicators; caregiver studies with both burden and satisfaction indicators. Longitudinal data preferred for causal inference. Exclude: datasets that contain only satisfaction OR only burden measures, or administrative records without subjective burden/satisfaction items.

variables.desc: Variables capturing both evaluative satisfaction and perceived burden/strain, plus mediators/moderators (coping, social support, resources).
variables.narr: Relevant variables: satisfaction measures (life/job/training) alongside burden indicators (perceived stress, burnout dimensions, workload, caregiver burden scores, psychological strain), coping strategies, social support, job control, health outcomes. Include variables enabling moderation/mediation analyses (resilience, resources). Exclude: objective workload metrics without subjective burden measures unless paired with satisfaction variables.

instruments_tools.desc: Validated scales and measurement tools for assessing satisfaction and burden/strain (stress, burnout, caregiver burden) and combined survey modules.
instruments_tools.narr: Relevant instruments: Satisfaction scales (SWLS, job satisfaction items) together with Perceived Stress Scale (PSS), Maslach Burnout Inventory (MBI), Copenhagen Burnout Inventory (CBI), Zarit Burden Interview (caregiver burden), workload and demand subscales; combined questionnaires and survey modules validated for assessing both constructs. Include psychometric documentation and recommended scoring procedures. Exclude: instruments that measure only objective workload or clinical diagnosis without validated subjective burden or satisfaction items.
